name: Konso

new_statements.quote: Konso has no lexical tone, and its functional load in the grammar is relatively light. It plays a minor role in verb conjugations, particularly in marking of a cleft object (§14.9.4) and the negative perfective (§14.5.2). Black & Shako (1973) indicate stress differences in their dictionary but this is erroneous; stress is not contrastive. [§14.2.2:] Word-final short vowels are devoiced (as in Oromo), except in the rare cases when they are high toned.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is explicitly non-contrastive (the stress marks in Black & Shako's 1973 dictionary are called erroneous). There is no lexical tone; a high tone has a small grammatical load only (cleft object marking, negative perfective, some person contrasts). No placement rule for word stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. The only prosodic detail is that word-final short vowels are devoiced except in the rare cases where they carry a (grammatical) high tone.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2023 chapter covers Konso (Afaa Xonso) as a whole and names four dialects (Faashe, Karatte, Tuuro, Xolme) without restricting the stress/tone statement to any one of them. Ongaye 2013 is a grammar of Konso by a native speaker (dialect base not checked for this task). Wondwosen 2020 treats the Konsoid cluster (Konso, Diraytata/Dirasha, Mosittacha) comparatively; only its Konso statements are relevant to kons1243.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two tone levels (L, H) with grammatical but no lexical function; the author leaves open whether the system is tone or pitch accent. The grammar contains no section on stress and the word 'stress' does not occur in the text (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text: only 'pitch accent' in the sentence quoted). Grammatical H marks the accusative in clefts (nominative L vs accusative H on the final vowel) and distinguishes 1SG present imperfective (final L) from 3 negative perfective / 1PL perfective (final H).

tone_statements.summary: Second-hand (source not named; Black 1974 for the reconstruction). Tone/accent has a morphological (verbal) role, none in gender marking; no word-level placement rule, consistent with the 9/12 snapshot (tonal-OR-pitch accent, no stress rule stated).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources opened. Ongaye & Mous 2023 (p. 229) and Ongaye 2013 (§2.9) agree that Konso has no lexical tone and only a light grammatical tone (H on cleft objects/accusative, negative perfective, some person contrasts); the 2023 chapter adds that stress is not contrastive. The 2023 chapter records one conflict with a source not opened here: Black & Shako's 1973 dictionary marks stress differences, which the chapter calls erroneous. Ongaye 2013 hedges the analysis as 'tone (or maybe pitch accent)' and says the system remains ill understood, so the type label (grammatical tone vs pitch accent) is not settled by the authors themselves, but neither source posits contrastive word stress or a stress placement rule.

audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal, non-strict; qv tonal-OR-pitch accent; domain not stated by the source) rests on the only full reference grammar of Konso (Ongaye 2013, LOT 326, 357 pp, native-speaker author), which we hold; the deciding quotation is verbatim at sec. 2.9 pp. 56-58 and the grammar never uses the word 'stress'. Glottolog (66 refs) and Crossref show no dedicated tone/stress/instrumental study of Konso; the 'phonology' entries in Glottolog concern Diraytata, not Konso. The open-access Wondwosen 2020 comparative phonology (downloaded) is consistent (H/L tone presupposed, no stress). The only unheld item that could sharpen the record is the same author's 2023 OUP handbook sketch (paywalled), which might settle 'tone vs pitch accent' wording but is unlikely to introduce a word-stress rule; the existing hedge (not in the strict set, qv tonal-OR-pitch accent) already encodes the author's own uncertainty. no reclassification

sources.citation: Wondwosen Tesfaye. 2020. The Comparative Phonology of Konsoid. Macrolinguistics 8(2) [serial 13]: 83-104. DOI 10.26478/ja2020.8.13.6 (open access).
sources.quote: Segmental comparison of Konso, Diraytata, Mosittacha; no stress or accent system is described for any of them. Tone enters only as a conditioning factor: 'in both Konso and Mosittacha, short vowels with a low tone are devoiced in word final positions ... whereas in Diraytata word final short vowels with a low tone are merged with zero' (citing Ongaye 2013:19 for Konso). Presupposes an H/L tone analysis for Konso; derivative of Ongaye 2013.
